words.ex: My study routine is simple: every evening after dinner, I learn ten new words.
Our teacher says we should read in English for at least fifteen minutes every day.
Our vocabulary test is on Monday, so on Sunday I'll revise all the words from Units 1 to 5 to make sure I still remember them.
My little brother can hear me from the next room when I practise English words aloud.
Everyone else was asleep on the night train to Bukhara, so I read my word list silently.
The teacher said 'vegetable' slowly, and the whole class had to repeat it three times.
I know what 'colleague' means, but I'm not sure about its pronunciation, so I listen to it in an online dictionary.
Dilnoza's history book is full of bright green lines, because she always reads with a highlighter in her hand.
When I read English news on my phone, I mark the new words with a star and look at them later.
Malika hears a new word on the bus, takes out her pen and writes it down in her notebook.
Under the new word 'nervous' I wrote an example sentence: 'I'm always nervous before exams.'
Our maths teacher says we must draw graphs in pencil, not in pen.
My answer in the crossword was wrong, so I rubbed it out and tried again.
Can I borrow your rubber? I wrote the wrong answer and I want to remove it.
In our English club nobody just sits and listens: everyone is active and speaks a lot.
Close your notebook and test yourself: how many of today's twenty words can you still remember?
Before you start the exercise, cover the answers at the bottom of the page with a piece of paper.
I know how to say this word, but what is its meaning?
I think 'village' means 'qishloq', but let me check in the dictionary.
I drew a diagram with the word 'school' in the middle and words like 'teacher' and 'desk' around it.
Mind maps help me organise new words into groups.
In my notebook I write 'heavy' as a common word partner of 'traffic'.
